# Motivation

## Nature is invisible in the accounts

- Ecosystems supply services the economy depends on, from pollination and soil retention to coastal protection and carbon storage, yet none of them appear in standard national accounts.
- Unmeasured, their loss shows up later as lower yields and higher damages.
- The Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP) account values what ecosystems supply, country by country and service by service, so natural capital can be tracked alongside GDP.
- The same service models also drive scenario analysis. They trace how climate and land-use scenarios change the services economies depend on, and the results feed the macroeconomic pipelines.

## Why one reviewed library

- Different contributors developed the GEP service models in different repos, each with its own layout, path conventions and aggregation choices.
- The library brings them into one repo with one layout. Every service runs the same way and writes the same per-country table the GEP account reads.
- The library gives policymakers a tool to price nature risk as the scenarios they use today carry no ecosystem-service feedback.

# What global_invest is

## One module per service

- The library holds one folder per ecosystem service, all on the same file convention.
- {{< meta n_services >}} services carry their GEP method in the library, with their input data in the shared base data.
- Some services also produce a scenario shock for the macroeconomic pipeline. A shock exists where the scenarios' physical changes (the land-use maps or the climate pathway) reach the service's science.
- The library is scenario agnostic. A caller supplies its own scenarios (the maps, the years and the naming) through configuration.

## How every GEP number is built

- Every service's number is the same construction. It multiplies a quantity of service delivered by a price and by nature's share of it, summed to one row per country.
- The three parts differ per service (recreation's quantity is visits and its price is travel cost, livestock's nature share is the ecosystem-provided part of feed), but the construction never changes, which is why one configuration table can describe every service.

## The code structure {.smaller}

| File | In paper terms |
|---|---|
| functions.py | The equations, pure science. |
| tasks.py | The estimation steps. Each writes one output. |
| initialize.py | The table of contents (the list of steps, and the entry point other pipelines call). |
| run_\<service\>.py | The main script. Opens a workspace and runs the steps. |
| method.qmd | The written explanation of the method. |
| results.qmd | The report of the results, rendered at the end of every run. |

- run_\<service\>.py asks initialize.py for the list of steps, each step in tasks.py calls the equations in functions.py and writes its output.
- A run ends by rendering results.qmd into a standalone HTML report for that service, carrying its total and the per-country table.
- A service with a shock has a second runner for it, run_\<service\>_shock.py.
- Three shared CSVs carry the configuration (next slide).

## The template every service follows

- Every run file lists the steps of its pipeline in one build_task_tree function.
- A service reads its settings from rows in three shared CSVs.
- es_config.csv: one row per service, with the GEP formula (quantity, price, attribution) plus the land base, the base year, the price convention and the crosswalk to the status sheet.
- es_scenarios_test.csv: the standard SEALS scenarios, with matching test maps shipped, so a standalone shock run works on any machine.
- es_parameters.csv: the run parameters and the references to each service's data.
- Every service reports one row per country (r250). The r264 table is the same 250 countries with fourteen disputed and overseas territories split out (India into six, China into four, and so on); it carries the map geometry and is what crosses with the AEZ zones the economic model needs. No account value is computed on it, and collapsing it back to r250 is a shared, tested step, because counting a split country once per sub-region is exactly how terrestrial carbon overstated its total by 23.5 percent.

## Automatic report by service {.smaller}

![Terrestrial carbon's report: its total, the same figures by income group, region and continent, the per-country table, and this map.](images/terrestrial_carbon_report_map.png)

- Seventeen of the twenty services with a run have rendered their report.

## The library's two callers

- Each service module serves two callers. The GEP account reads the valuation (one row per country), and the macroeconomic pipeline reads the scenario shock (a table of productivity deviations).
- Both read the same functions file, so a change to the science reaches both callers at once.

# Where things stand

## The state in numbers

- The test of whether a service is ours is whether we can run it: our own code, read, rewritten and tested here. 22 of the {{< meta n_services >}} produce their number that way today, and the 23rd, erosion, is running.
- No service is waiting on a file from anyone. Erosion was the last one we called blocked, on four upstream layers at a cluster path we cannot reach. Those four are diagnostics the run does not need, and the one layer it does need we now build ourselves from the elevation model. Every erosion input is in the shared base data, and the run is going.
- Two run but carry one borrowed component each: coastal protection computes its mangrove half and reads its coral half, and water quality computes its dollar figures and reads its international-dollar headline. Those two components are the only numbers left with no code here to run.
- Running our code is one thing, checking it against someone else's is another. {{< meta n_replicating >}} of our runs land on a committed reference or the manuscript. {{< meta n_awaiting_file >}} have nothing to check against, because no reference output exists: recreation, commercial fisheries, landslide, non-timber forest products and stormwater. Erosion's run is ongoing.
- Livestock now computes both attributions and they are far apart. The same $2.29T of gross production gives $519bn through the CWoN land rental rate and {{< meta livestock_world >}} through the GLEAM feed share, a factor of 2.6. Which factor the account uses is a decision, not a gap.

## What the status sheet's columns mean {.smaller}

- Every service is built the same way, in two files. One holds the maths and never opens or saves anything, so any step in it can be called with a few made-up numbers and checked against an answer worked out by hand, which is what the tests do. The other does the reading and writing: it loads the input data, calls the maths, and writes the results.
- Keeping them apart is what lets a service be tested without a global dataset, and it is why a run and a test can only ever disagree about the data.
- The sheet's columns follow from that. A dash means the field does not apply.
- The methods are not settled. Every service has a method page in its own folder, and those pages are work in progress: some describe a calculation we have since changed, two of them described a different service entirely until today, and several leave the attribution factor open. Read the method column for what the code does now, and the page for the reasoning, but do not treat either as decided.

| column | what it holds |
|---|---|
| method | how the number is computed, in one line |
| code | the engineering work we did |
| number | what the figure is, and what it was checked against |
| need | what we are waiting on from someone else |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,82]"}

# Open questions by service

## terrestrial_carbon

- [Values carbon stored by land ecosystems: a zone-by-class density table on the land-cover map, priced at the rental social cost of carbon. Our run reproduces the manuscript's total, once a double-count that entered split countries once per sub-region (China six times, overstating the total by 23.5 percent) was fixed.]{.state}
- **Q1:** do carbon prices grow, and at what rate? The rental is P(1 - e^-r) where r is the net rate, the discount rate minus the growth rate of carbon prices, so our 2 percent column assumes prices do not grow. The table already holds the alternative: 3 percent discounting minus 2.2 percent growth, so 0.8 percent net, giving $2.29 a tonne against our $13.19. That choice moves the account by more than the gap between 2 and 3 percent.
- **Q2:** is the 1 percent sensitivity wanted? The 3 percent one is a run of its own and gives {{< meta terrestrial_total_r3 >}} against {{< meta terrestrial_total >}}, but 1 percent cannot be produced from what we hold. The table holds two prices, $181.60 per tonne of CO2 at 2 percent and $78.53 at 3 percent, typed in rather than computed, with no record of where they came from. Every other cell follows from those two by arithmetic. Nor can it be reasoned to: two present values do not determine the damage path behind them, and three paths that fit both anchors exactly give 16 times the base price at 1 percent, 29 times, or no finite value.

## coastal_carbon

- [Values carbon stored in mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass: mapped habitat times per-habitat density, priced like terrestrial carbon. Computed in the library from the habitat maps, and it reproduces the author's reported numbers.]{.state}
- **Q1:** was EEZ-only chosen to avoid double-counting the landward pixels with terrestrial carbon? Most of the mapped habitat sits landward of the shoreline (97.5 percent of mangrove area, 84 percent of salt marsh), so including it multiplies the total by 4.5.
- **Q2:** which exact seagrass and salt marsh input versions produced the report's {{< meta coastal_report >}}? Our replication gives {{< meta coastal_eez >}} with the mangrove component matching, and the report's own seagrass area (62.21 Mha) exceeds the published range it cites (16 to 26.7 Mha).
- **Q3:** if both sides count, a landward mask must prevent double-counting with terrestrial carbon. Does one exist?

## marine_carbon

- [The service sheet lists Terrestrial, Coastal, and Marine carbon. No marine module found in any repo.]{.state}
- **Q1:** is marine carbon in scope for the account?
- **Q2:** if yes, which data drives it?
- **Q3:** most open-ocean carbon sits in the high seas, inside no country's EEZ. Which attribution convention should a per-country account use?
- The sheet lists one more subgroup under the same service, Other Non-Carbon GHG. We could not find a module for it either, and the same three questions apply.

## pollination

- [Values crop production attributable to wild pollinators, from a sufficiency-weighted value raster built from pollinator habitat around cropland. We aggregate that raster to countries ourselves. It is a 2023 raster, and we regenerate it at 2019 once the definition is decided.]{.state}
- **Q1:** is pollination's value the service nature currently delivers ({{< meta poll_raster >}}, the sufficiency-weighted raster) or the production value at stake ({{< meta poll_fao >}}, dependence-weighted FAO value)? The country ranking is identical.
- **Q2:** does the account add pollination on top of crop_provision? Crop multiplies production value by the land rental rate, so both attribute part of the same output to nature.

## erosion

- [Values soil the land cover keeps in place: prevented erosion mapped by running the sediment-delivery model ourselves, valued through crop productivity. It is running for the first time, and we report no number until it lands.]{.state}
- **Q1:** which of the three shock methods is the account's? We compute damage (thresholded area share), service (threshold-free and magnitude-weighted per crop) and service-threshold (service restricted to a fixed severe-pixel set) side by side.

## landslide_mitigation

- [Values landslide deaths avoided by forest cover: slope stability modelled with and without forest root cohesion, the difference turned into avoided deaths and priced at a value of a statistical life. Computed end to end in the library.]{.state}
- **Q1:** do you have a per-country output from a v0.2.0 run?
- **Q2:** which input versions did the run behind the v0.2.0 release use?

## fisheries

- [Values commercial capture fisheries as the economic rent of the catch, and subsistence fisheries as the consumptive-use value of home catch. The commercial rent is computed in the library from the CWoN tables. The subsistence component reports the published per-country values, and reproduces them exactly.]{.state}
- **Q1:** should the RCP8.5-for-RCP7.0 substitution stand?
- **Q2:** which CWoN vintage produced the shock file (cwon_shocks.har)?
- **Q3:** should the account's fisheries value come from the CWoN resource rents or from the FishStatJ catch pipeline? Is there a per-country CSV from the run of the CWoN script?
- **Q4:** does the subsistence value add to the commercial number, or does that number already contain the subsistence catch? Where FAO catch statistics already include subsistence fishing, summing the two counts it twice.

## recreation

- [Values visits to natural recreation sites at travel cost: 1 km sites ranked by land-cover shares, protected areas and road access, then a gravity model sends residents on day trips and tourists on overnight stays into the high-quality sites. Computed end to end in the library.]{.state}
- **Q1:** where can we find the source pipeline's results_by_country.csv?
- **Q2:** did the travel-cost step intend km? It multiplies a USD-per-km fuel cost by a distance measured in the raster's pixel units (degrees), which understates values.

## crop_provision

- [Values crop production from FAOSTAT production values, quantity times producer price per country, times the land rental rate. We run it ourselves and it replicates, validated against the reference table.]{.state}
- **Q1:** does the account add crop_provision and pollination? Both attribute part of the same output to nature.
- **Q2:** is subsistence in scope as a separate crop subgroup? Adding it would double-count, because FAOSTAT's production values already include part of what households grow and eat themselves.

## livestock_provision

- [Values livestock production and attributes to nature the share of feed ecosystems provide. Both attributions now run: on $2.29T of gross production over the 65 FAO item codes, the CWoN land rental rate gives $519bn and the GLEAM feed share gives {{< meta livestock_world >}}, a factor of 2.6. India recovers from zero to {{< meta livestock_ind >}} on the item list alone.]{.state}
- **Q1:** which factor does the account attribute with, the land rental rate or the feed share? They differ by 2.6 times. The rental rate belongs to the crop method, and this service's own method page defines it as the factor, but that page is the crop method page, referring to crop items throughout.
- **Q2:** should milk and the other missing products count as livestock production? The library's old list covered meat and eggs only and captured 4 percent of India's FAO livestock value, while the method repo's list of 65 products includes milk.
- **Q3:** can you share the GLEAM 3 intake extract (gleam3_dmi.xlsx) to check ours against, and a per-country output? We have harvested the intake from FAO's public dashboard for 231 countries, 205 matching a country in the account, and it does carry all eight feed categories, shown a different subset per species. So we compute the feed share; what we lack is anything to validate it against.
## coastal_protection

- [Values storm damage that mangroves and coral reefs prevent along coastlines. The {{< meta cp_total >}} is the sum of two halves that stand differently. Mangroves are ours: hectares times value per hectare gives $30,400,076,961 against the table's $30,400,082,253, a difference of $5,291 that is its own per-row rounding. Corals are not: that file carries a finished benefit per country with nothing underneath it, $5.17bn at 2011, and we only carry it to the base year with a deflator, making it $6.32bn.]{.state}
- **Q1:** is there code behind the coral-reef benefit table that we should be running? That half is still someone else's number, so a disagreement with it could not surface.
- **Q2:** should the 9 countries missing from the deflator table be left unvalued rather than zero? They are currently zeroed by the join, which reads as no damage prevented.

## extractive_materials

- [Values mineral extraction as the resource-rent share of mining output. Computed in the library from the World Bank rent and GDP tables, and our run reproduces the reference per country.]{.state}
- **Q1:** what is the source of the {{< meta extractive_factor >}} factor? The valuation multiplies mineral rents times GDP by it, and without it the total would be {{< meta extractive_alt >}} instead of {{< meta extractive_total >}}.
- **Q2:** should the 9 countries with no World Bank rent data stay unvalued rather than zero? We leave them empty today, which is the convention the group's guidance asks us to confirm.

## renewable_energy

- [Values wind, solar and geothermal electricity as generation times price times a resource-rent share. Our run gives {{< meta renewable_wind >}} wind, {{< meta renewable_solar >}} solar and {{< meta renewable_geothermal >}} geothermal, and a fresh run reproduces each to the cent.]{.state}
- **Q1:** which is current, the code's {{< meta renewable_total >}} or the drive CSVs' {{< meta renewable_ref >}}?
- **Q2:** should wind, solar and geothermal be three services in the account or one? The sheet lists three, the library computes them together and already writes a table per resource, so either shape is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

## fire_protection

- [Values wildfire damage avoided by nature's fire regulation: a per-country fire-persistence coefficient times the country's 2018 burned area gives avoided acres in 2019, valued at EM-DAT damage per burned acre. Our run reproduces the source repo's committed output for all 161 countries.]{.state}
- **Q1:** which of the three coefficients is the account's value? They disagree in sign: baseline persistence gives {{< meta fire_baseline_total >}}, the nature-versus-human cause difference {{< meta fire_cause_total >}}, and the nature-versus-human area difference {{< meta fire_area_total >}}.
- **Q2:** should the 89 countries the regressions do not cover stay unvalued? No data is not zero avoided damage.

## water_supply

- [Values hydropower rent and priced water withdrawal. Hydropower is computed from the CWoN wealth table for every country it values, {{< meta water_supply_total >}} across 112 countries, and reproduces the drive's committed output exactly on the 95 countries that output covers. Water use is computed in the library, agriculture {{< meta water_use_ag_total >}} across 126 countries and all-sector {{< meta water_use_all_total >}} across 154.]{.state}
- **Q1:** which hydropower total is the account's, the manuscript's {{< meta hydro_manuscript >}} or our rent-based {{< meta water_supply_total >}}? The first follows a direct-use method, price times generation, the second the resource-rent method.
- **Q2:** why does the reference leave 17 countries empty although the CWoN table values them? We now report all 112, and carry the 95-country variant beside it as the comparison, so the {{< meta water_supply_anchor >}} anchor still checks out.
- **Q3:** what attribution step turns water use into a nature share? The all-sector total is the gross economic value of water use, close to global GDP.
- **Q4:** how do hydropower and the two water-use components combine into one water_supply value?

- [Values deaths avoided by vegetation capturing air pollution, priced at a GDP-adjusted value of a statistical life (the monetary value assigned to one avoided death). We recompute the valuation and reproduce the committed totals. The avoided-death counts come from the group's emissions-to-health model, which turns fire emissions into excess deaths; we do not rebuild it and take its counts as given.]{.state}
- **Q1:** which VSL build produced the committed value column? The method is documented (US-anchored, adjusted for GDP and life-years) but the raw data shipped beside it is a different vintage and does not reproduce the column.

- [Values deaths avoided by ecosystems suppressing windblown dust, priced the same way as air filtration and computed by the same module. We recompute the valuation and reproduce the committed totals.]{.state}

- [Values flood damage avoided by ecosystems: flood depth by return period, depth-damage functions and the asset map give each country's expected annual damage. Our recompute reproduces the pipeline's table for 146 of 148 non-zero countries.]{.state}

## local_climate_regulation

- [Values cooling energy avoided by urban vegetation: an urban cooling model gives each city-month a cooling effect, priced at national electricity prices. We now sum the city files ourselves, {{< meta lcr_ours >}} across 177 countries, instead of reading the committed table.]{.state}
- **Q1:** what turns those city valuations into the committed accounting table's {{< meta lcr_committed >}}? The gap is not a constant factor, ranging from about 2.5 to 766 across countries, so it is not a units slip.

## extractive_energy

- [Values fossil-fuel resource rents (gas, coal and petroleum) at 2019, on the same commodity convention extractive_materials uses. Computed in the library from the public CWoN rent tables the method appendices name.]{.state}
- **Q1:** are the eight duplicated rows in the committed tables a join error, and which total does the account keep? Christmas Island and Cocos carry Australia's rents, Bouvet and Svalbard Norway's, Tokelau New Zealand's, Western Sahara Morocco's, Palestine Israel's and Kosovo Serbia's, so the committed {{< meta xe_committed >}} counts those countries twice. One country one row gives {{< meta xe_total >}}.

## timber_provision

- [Values timber harvests net of harvest and transport costs. Our reimplementation matches the committed output for all 166 countries.]{.state}
- **Q1:** is there a forest-management mask behind the value raster, or code that builds one? We can sum that raster to countries and match it exactly, but we cannot make our own: the mask saying which forest is available for harvest is not derivable from the layers we hold.

## ntfp

- [Values non-timber forest products as accessible forest area (near roads and rivers) times the CWoN value per hectare. Ours end to end: $19.86bn over 142 countries, from 2,590 million accessible hectares, which is 64 percent of the world's forest lying within 10 km of a road or river. No reference output exists to check it against.]{.state}
- **Q1:** should the price be rescaled to the accessible area, or should accessibility not restrict the quantity? CWoN spreads its annual value over its own forest area and we multiply it by the smaller accessible area, so the same forest is being valued at two different extents.
## stormwater

- [Values stormwater retained by urban vegetation and soils. Our own retention run on the drive's configuration retains {{< meta stormwater_volume >}} per year across 104 countries, wall to wall rather than urban-masked, and the module prices that volume. The run and the country step sit beside the task tree rather than inside it.]{.state}
- **Q1:** what is the intended price per cubic metre retained? The configuration carries a placeholder of 1, so today's value is the volume.
- **Q2:** should the run be masked to urban areas? It currently covers the whole land surface.

# Appendix

## How a run finds its data

- Every input is a reference path relative to the shared base data, and each machine resolves it for itself: the task's own directory first (so finished work is found and skipped), then the project's input folder, then the machine's base_data, then the cloud fallback.
- A run therefore carries no absolute paths. The same run file works on a laptop, on the cluster, or on any machine that stages the same base data.
- Tasks cache their output in the project directory and skip themselves when it already exists, so a rerun recomputes nothing and an interrupted run resumes where it stopped.

## How a pipeline grafts a service

- A caller grafts a service with one call (add_\<service\>_tasks(p) after its land-use step), and the service's tasks slot into the caller's own task tree.
- A CSV cell is a default. The caller's configuration prevails over the shipped CSVs, so the library never needs to know its callers' naming.
